hints: Look closely at the starting materials, are they compounds or elements in their standard states?
Recall that forming one mole of a compound from its elements is the definition of standard enthalpy of formation, and here you make 2 moles of $\text{CO}_2$ and 3 moles of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
Check both the type of enthalpy symbol and the exact state symbols, liquid water is different from steam and formation is different from combustion.
walkthrough:
**Identify what type of reaction this is**

Look at the reactants: $\text{C(s)}$, $\text{H}_2\text{(g)}$ and $\text{O}_2\text{(g)}$. These are all elements in their standard states.

They react to form compounds: $\text{CO}_2\text{(g)}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$.

**Recall the definition of standard enthalpy of formation**

Standard enthalpy of formation, $\Delta H_f^\ominus$, is the enthalpy change when 1 mole of a compound is formed from its elements under standard conditions.

$$\text{elements in standard states} \rightarrow \text{1 mol compound}$$

**Apply the definition to this equation**

Here we do not make 1 mole, we make 2 moles of $\text{CO}_2$ and 3 moles of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$. So Q is just the sum of those formation enthalpies.

$$Q = 2 \times \Delta H_f^\ominus[\text{CO}_2\text{(g)}] + 3 \times \Delta H_f^\ominus[\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}]$$

**Match states and symbols carefully**

The water product is liquid, so we must use $\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$, not $\text{H}_2\text{O(g)}$. And we must use formation, $\Delta H_f^\ominus$, not combustion, $\Delta H_c^\ominus$. This gives the correct expression.

options.A: Incorrect. This mixes $\Delta H_c^\ominus$ for $\text{CO}_2$ with $\Delta H_f^\ominus$ for $\text{H}_2$. Combustion enthalpy is defined for burning 1 mole in oxygen, not for forming from elements. The reaction shown is formation from elements, not combustion.
options.B: Incorrect. This has two errors. It uses $\text{H}_2\text{O(g)}$ instead of $\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$, and state symbols matter because condensing gas to liquid releases energy. It also wrongly uses $\Delta H_c^\ominus$ for $\text{CO}_2$ instead of $\Delta H_f^\ominus$.
options.C: Incorrect. This only includes the $\text{CO}_2$ formation term and wrongly subtracts a term for $\text{H}_2$. Remember $\Delta H_f^\ominus$ of an element in its standard state like $\text{H}_2\text{(g)}$ is zero, and you must also add the formation enthalpy for all 3 moles of $\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$.
options.D: Correct. Reactants are all elements in standard states forming 2 moles of $\text{CO}_2\text{(g)}$ and 3 moles of $\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}$. So Q equals the sum of the standard formation enthalpies: $3 \times \Delta H_f^\ominus[\text{H}_2\text{O(l)}] + 2 \times \Delta H_f^\ominus[\text{CO}_2\text{(g)}]$.
